title: How Much Alcohol Is Too Much? Daily, Weekly and One-Night Limits
excerpt: How much alcohol is too much? The official daily, weekly, and one-night limits from the US, UK, Canada, and WHO, what counts as one drink, and the warning signs that need help.
metaDescription: How much alcohol is too much? Daily, weekly, and one-night drinking limits from US, UK, and WHO guidance, what counts as a drink, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: how much alcohol is too much
content:
**The short answer:** for most healthy adults, US guidance treats more than 4 drinks in a day or 14 in a week as too much for men, and more than 3 in a day or 7 in a week as too much for women. In a single night, about 5 drinks for men or 4 for women within two hours counts as binge drinking. Newer health guidance goes further and says that less is better at every level, because the risk of some cancers starts climbing from the first regular drink. This guide explains what a "drink" actually is, how the different countries draw their lines, what changes for your own body, and the warning signs that mean someone needs help right now.

**The quick rules:** Count in standard drinks, not glasses. Stay under the daily and weekly limits below. Don't drink more than about one standard drink per hour. Keep several alcohol-free days each week. Skip alcohol entirely if you're pregnant, driving, under 21 in the US, or taking a medication that interacts with it.

> **This is not medical advice.** These are general guidelines for healthy adults, not personal limits. Your safe amount may be lower, or zero, if you take certain medications, have liver disease, a heart condition, diabetes, a history of seizures, or a personal or family history of alcohol problems. **Call 911 right away if** someone who has been drinking is confused, can't be woken up, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. **See a doctor soon if** you regularly drink more than the limits below, find it hard to cut back, or feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or sick when you go without a drink. Stopping suddenly after heavy daily drinking can be dangerous, so get medical advice before quitting cold turkey.

## First, What Counts as "One Drink"?

Every guideline in this article is measured in **standard drinks**, and most people underestimate how many they're having. In the US, a standard drink is any drink that contains about **14 grams of pure alcohol**. That works out to:

- **12 oz of regular beer** (about 5% alcohol)
- **8 to 9 oz of malt liquor** (about 7%)
- **5 oz of wine** (about 12%)
- **1.5 oz of spirits** (a single shot of 40% vodka, whiskey, gin, rum, or tequila)

Here's where people go wrong. A typical restaurant pour of wine is often 6 to 9 oz, not 5. A pint of 7% IPA is closer to two standard drinks than one. A cocktail like a Long Island iced tea or a strong margarita can hold two or three shots. A 750 ml bottle of 12% wine contains about five standard drinks, so splitting one with a friend is roughly two and a half drinks each. Our guide to [what counts as a standard drink](/never-hungover/what-is-a-standard-drink) has the full chart by drink type.

If you want to check your usual drinks, our guide to [alcohol content by drink](/never-hungover/alcohol-content-by-drink) breaks down common beers, wines, and cocktails, and [how many drinks are in a bottle of wine](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-in-a-bottle-of-wine) covers the most common pour-size trap.

One more wrinkle: other countries define a "drink" differently. A UK **unit** is 8 grams of alcohol, so one US standard drink is about 1.75 UK units. A Canadian standard drink is about 13.5 grams, close to the US one. When you compare guidelines between countries, keep these different sizes in mind.

## How Much Alcohol Is Too Much? The Official Guidelines Side by Side

Different health agencies draw the line in slightly different places, but they all point the same way. Here's how the major guidelines compare for healthy, non-pregnant adults.

| Source | Daily guidance | Weekly guidance | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **US Dietary Guidelines (2020 to 2025 edition)** | Men: up to 2 drinks. Women: up to 1 drink. | Not set as a weekly number | Described as the limit for "moderate" drinking on days you drink, not a target. |
| **NIAAA (US)** | Heavy if more than 4 (men) or more than 3 (women) on any day | Heavy if more than 14 (men) or more than 7 (women) a week | Both the daily and the weekly limit matter. |
| **CDC (US)** | Binge: 5+ (men) or 4+ (women) on one occasion | Heavy: 15+ (men) or 8+ (women) a week | Used to define "excessive drinking." |
| **UK Chief Medical Officers (2016)** | No daily figure; avoid heavy single sessions | No more than 14 units (about 8 US drinks) for everyone | Spread over 3 or more days, with several drink-free days. |
| **Canada's Guidance on Alcohol and Health (2023)** | No more than 2 drinks on any occasion | 1 to 2 a week: low risk. 3 to 6: moderate. 7+: increasingly high. | Built mainly around long-term cancer risk. |
| **World Health Organization (2023)** | No safe level identified | No safe level identified | Says risk starts with the first drink. |

Notice the trend. Older guidance focused on a daily amount that seemed acceptable. Newer guidance, especially Canada's and the WHO's, frames alcohol as a sliding scale of risk where fewer drinks always means lower risk. The US has been moving the same way: in early 2025 the US Surgeon General issued an advisory on alcohol and cancer, calling alcohol a leading preventable cause of cancer in the US and recommending clearer cancer warnings on labels.

None of these limits are "safe amounts" you should aim for. They're ceilings. Under them, risk is lower. Over them, risk rises faster.

## How Many Drinks a Day Is Too Much?

If you use the US numbers, the daily line looks like this:

- **Men:** up to 2 drinks on a drinking day is considered moderate. More than 4 in one day counts as heavy drinking for that day.
- **Women:** up to 1 drink on a drinking day is considered moderate. More than 3 in one day counts as heavy drinking for that day.

The gap between "moderate" and "heavy" is a gray zone. Two or three drinks a day for a woman, or three or four for a man, isn't an emergency, but it's above what most guidance calls low risk, especially if it happens often.

The daily limit also isn't a weekly allowance you can save up. Having zero drinks Monday through Friday and then eight on Saturday isn't the same as one drink a day. The single big night carries the risks of a binge (accidents, injuries, alcohol poisoning, bad decisions, a brutal hangover) even though your weekly total looks fine on paper.

## How Many Drinks a Week Is Too Much?

Weekly totals matter most for long-term health: liver disease, high blood pressure, heart rhythm problems, and several cancers all track with how much you drink over months and years.

- **US (NIAAA):** more than 14 drinks a week for men or more than 7 for women is heavy drinking.
- **UK:** no more than 14 units a week for anyone. Because UK units are smaller, that's only about 8 US standard drinks a week, or roughly 6 pints of average beer or 6 medium glasses of wine.
- **Canada:** 2 drinks or fewer a week is low risk. Risk becomes moderate at 3 to 6 and increasingly high from 7 up.

So someone who has two glasses of wine every evening (likely 10 to 14 oz, or 2 to 3 standard drinks) is at 14 to 21 drinks a week. That's over the NIAAA weekly line for women, at or over it for men, and well over the UK and Canadian guidance. Daily habits add up faster than most people expect, which is why it's worth counting for a week or two.

## How Much Alcohol Is Too Much in One Night?

For a single night out, the key concept is **binge drinking**. NIAAA defines it as a pattern of drinking that brings your blood alcohol concentration (BAC) to 0.08% or higher, which is the legal driving limit in most US states. For a typical adult, that happens after about:

- **5 or more drinks for men** in about 2 hours
- **4 or more drinks for women** in about 2 hours

The reason speed matters so much: your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for an average adult. You can't speed that up with coffee, water, food, or a cold shower. Any drink beyond that pace piles up in your blood. That's why four drinks spread over a long dinner affect you very differently from four shots in 30 minutes. Our guides on [how many drinks it takes to get drunk](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-to-get-drunk) and [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explain the timing in more detail.

Past the binge threshold, the risks stack up quickly: falls, car crashes, blackouts, unprotected sex, fights, and alcohol poisoning. Memory gaps are a clear sign you've gone well past your limit; our article on [blackouts](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) explains what's happening in the brain when that happens.

## Is There a Safe Amount of Alcohol?

This is where the science has shifted most in recent years.

For decades, people heard that a drink a day might be good for the heart. Much of that evidence came from observational studies that compared moderate drinkers with non-drinkers. The problem is that the "non-drinker" group often included former drinkers who had quit because of illness, which made light drinkers look healthier by comparison. More careful analyses have weakened the case for any heart benefit.

Meanwhile, the evidence on cancer has grown stronger. Alcohol is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen (a substance known to cause cancer) by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, and it's linked to cancers of the mouth, throat, esophagus, liver, colon, rectum, and breast. For breast cancer in particular, risk rises even at about one drink a day.

That's why the WHO stated in 2023 that no level of alcohol use is safe for health. It's an important message, but it's easy to misread. It does **not** mean a glass of wine at a wedding is dangerous. It means:

- Risk starts low and rises with every additional drink, especially over the long term.
- There's no threshold below which risk is exactly zero.
- Drinking less is better for health than drinking more, at every level.

For most social drinkers, the practical takeaway is simple. Fewer drinks, fewer drinking days, and no binges will lower your risk no matter where you start.

## Is Drinking Every Night Too Much?

A single drink every night is within the older US limit for men and right at the limit for women. Under the UK and Canadian guidance, seven or more drinks a week already sits in a higher risk band. But the bigger issue with nightly drinking isn't one drink. It's what tends to happen over time:

- **The amount drifts up.** One glass becomes a generous glass, then two.
- **Tolerance builds.** You need more to feel the same effect, which is a sign your body is adapting to regular alcohol.
- **Sleep suffers.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up the second half of the night, so you wake less rested even after one or two drinks.
- **Your liver never gets a break.** Fat can start to build up in the liver with regular heavy drinking, and early fatty liver usually causes no symptoms.

Both the UK and Canadian guidance recommend several alcohol-free days each week. A good self-check is to take a few nights off. If that's easy, great. If it feels surprisingly hard, or you feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or unable to sleep without a drink, that's worth raising with a doctor. Those can be early signs of physical dependence, and it's much easier to address early.

## What Changes Your Personal Limit?

Guidelines are written for an average healthy adult. Your real limit may be lower because of:

### Sex and body size

Women generally reach a higher blood alcohol level than men from the same drink. On average they have less body water to dilute alcohol, and differences in how alcohol is broken down also play a role. Smaller people of either sex are affected more by the same amount.

### Age

As you get older, your body holds less water, your liver processes alcohol more slowly, and you're more likely to take medications that interact with it. Older adults also have higher risk of falls. NIAAA suggests that adults over 65 who drink keep it to about one drink a day at most.

### Medications

Many common medicines don't mix well with alcohol, including acetaminophen, sleep aids, antihistamines, opioids, anxiety medications, some antidepressants, blood thinners, and diabetes medications. If a label says to avoid alcohol, the limit for you is zero, or whatever your doctor or pharmacist tells you.

### Health conditions

Liver disease, pancreatitis, heart rhythm problems, high blood pressure, diabetes, a history of seizures, depression, or anxiety can all lower the amount that's reasonable for you.

### Genetics and flushing

People who get a red, hot face after a drink often carry a variant of the ALDH2 gene, common in people of East Asian descent, that slows the breakdown of acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol. Research links this flushing reaction with higher risk of esophageal cancer when people with it drink regularly. If you flush, it's a strong reason to keep drinking light.

### Food, water, and pace

Drinking on an empty stomach makes alcohol hit your bloodstream faster and peak higher. Eating before and during drinking and alternating with water slows things down, though it doesn't change how fast your liver clears what you've had.

## When Zero Is the Right Amount

For some people and situations, the guidance is clear: no alcohol at all.

- **If you're pregnant or trying to become pregnant.** No safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy is known.
- **Before driving, operating machinery, swimming, or doing anything that needs full coordination.**
- **If you're under the legal drinking age.**
- **If you take a medication that interacts with alcohol.**
- **If you have certain conditions** such as liver disease or pancreatitis, or your doctor has told you to avoid it.
- **If you're in recovery or can't control how much you drink once you start.**

## Signs You Might Be Drinking Too Much

Numbers aside, your own experience is a good guide. Consider talking with a doctor if several of these sound familiar:

- You regularly go over the daily or weekly limits above.
- You often drink more, or for longer, than you meant to.
- You've tried to cut back and found it hard.
- You need more drinks than you used to for the same effect.
- You've had memory gaps after drinking.
- Hangovers are costing you work, plans, or time with people you care about.
- Friends or family have mentioned your drinking.
- You feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, irritable, or sick when you haven't had a drink, and a drink makes it better.

Many doctors use a short three-question screen called the **AUDIT-C**, which asks how often you drink, how many drinks you have on a typical day, and how often you have six or more at once. NIAAA's "Rethinking Drinking" website has free tools to check your pattern and plan changes. A primary care doctor is a good, judgment-free place to start; this is a routine health conversation, the same as one about blood pressure.

## When Too Much Becomes an Emergency

Alcohol poisoning happens when there's so much alcohol in the blood that the parts of the brain controlling breathing, heart rate, and temperature start to shut down. It's most common after fast drinking, drinking games, and shots. **Call 911 if someone who has been drinking:**

- Is confused or can't be woken up
- Is vomiting while drowsy or passed out
- Has slow breathing (fewer than 8 breaths a minute) or gaps of 10 seconds or more between breaths
- Has a seizure
- Has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin, or a low body temperature

Don't let them "sleep it off." Their BAC can keep rising after they stop drinking, because alcohol is still being absorbed from the stomach. Stay with them, turn them on their side so they don't choke if they vomit, and don't give them coffee or a cold shower. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) covers what to do in more detail.

The other urgent situation is **withdrawal**. If someone has been drinking heavily every day and stops suddenly, they can develop tremors, sweating, a racing heart, vomiting, hallucinations, or seizures, usually within a day or two. That needs medical care. If this describes you, talk to a doctor before stopping, so it can be done safely.

## Practical Ways to Stay Under Your Limit

You don't need a big lifestyle overhaul to drink less. Small habits do most of the work:

1. **Decide your number before you go out.** It's much easier to stick to a plan you made sober.
2. **Count standard drinks, not glasses.** A big wine pour or a strong IPA can be two drinks.
3. **Pace yourself at about one drink an hour or slower.** Sip, don't shoot.
4. **Alternate with water or a non-alcoholic drink.** It slows you down and keeps you hydrated.
5. **Eat a real meal first.** Protein, fat, and fiber slow alcohol absorption.
6. **Pick lower-strength options.** A 4% beer instead of an 8% double IPA, or a wine spritzer instead of a full glass.
7. **Plan alcohol-free days.** Aim for several each week, as UK and Canadian guidance suggest.
8. **Skip drinking games and rounds.** Rounds push everyone to drink at the fastest person's pace.
9. **Track your week.** An app or a note on your phone shows patterns you won't notice otherwise.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) has more on pacing, food, and hydration for nights you do drink.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people take DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, on nights they drink. Lab and animal research suggests it may support the enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde and may affect how alcohol acts on the brain, and some people find they feel better the next morning. Human research is still limited, so keep expectations modest.

What DHM does **not** do is change any of the limits in this guide. There is no good evidence that DHM, or any supplement, makes heavy drinking safe, reduces the long-term cancer or liver risks of alcohol, or lowers your blood alcohol level enough to drive. It is not a way to drink more.

If you've already decided to have a moderate night and want to try DHM, two widely used options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and if you take any regular medication, check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

For healthy adults, US guidance draws the line at more than 4 drinks a day or 14 a week for men, and more than 3 a day or 7 a week for women. For a single night, 5 or more drinks for men or 4 or more for women in about two hours is a binge. Stricter guidance from the UK, Canada, and the WHO adds that lower is better at every level, mainly because of cancer risk. In practice, the safest pattern for people who choose to drink is a few standard drinks a week, never more than one an hour, several alcohol-free days, and no binges. If you're regularly over these numbers, find it hard to cut back, or feel unwell when you stop, a doctor can help you sort out what's right for you.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How much alcohol is too much in one day?**

Under US guidance from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), more than 4 drinks in a day for men or more than 3 for women counts as heavy drinking for that day. The US Dietary Guidelines have long set a lower bar for moderate drinking: up to 2 drinks a day for men and 1 for women. A drink here means a standard drink with about 14 grams of pure alcohol, such as 12 oz of 5% beer, 5 oz of 12% wine, or 1.5 oz of 40% spirits.

**How many drinks a week is too much?**

NIAAA treats more than 14 drinks a week for men or more than 7 for women as heavy drinking, and the CDC uses 15 or more for men and 8 or more for women. The UK advises no more than 14 units a week for anyone (about 6 pints of average-strength beer or 6 medium glasses of wine), spread over three or more days. Canada's 2023 guidance is stricter: 1 to 2 drinks a week is low risk, 3 to 6 is moderate risk, and 7 or more carries increasingly high risk.

**How much alcohol is too much in one night?**

Drinking that brings your blood alcohol to 0.08% or higher counts as binge drinking. For most adults that's about 5 or more drinks for men or 4 or more for women within roughly 2 hours. Your body clears about one standard drink an hour, so stacking drinks faster than that lets alcohol build up in your blood. Signs like confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, or being hard to wake mean the person needs emergency help now.

**Is there a safe amount of alcohol?**

The World Health Organization said in 2023 that no level of drinking is safe for health, mainly because alcohol raises the risk of several cancers starting at low amounts. That doesn't mean one drink is dangerous. It means risk starts low and climbs as you drink more, and there's no amount that is risk-free. For many people the practical goal is to keep drinking low, avoid binges, and have several alcohol-free days a week.

**Is drinking every night bad for you?**

It depends on how much. One drink with dinner every night is within older US moderate-drinking limits for men and right at the edge for women, but daily drinking makes it easier for the amount to creep up, builds tolerance, and gives your liver no days off. The UK and Canadian guidance both recommend several alcohol-free days a week. If you find it hard to skip a night, or feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you do, talk to a doctor.

**Why are the limits lower for women?**

On average, women have less body water than men of the same weight, so the same drink produces a higher blood alcohol level. Differences in body size and in how alcohol is broken down in the stomach and liver also play a part. That's why US guidance sets lower daily and weekly limits for women. The UK chose one limit for everyone, set low enough to cover both.

**What are the signs I'm drinking too much?**

Common signs include regularly going over the daily or weekly limits, drinking more or longer than you planned, needing more to feel the same effect, blackouts, hangovers that cost you work or plans, and feeling shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you haven't had a drink. Short screening questionnaires such as the AUDIT-C, used by many doctors, can give you a quick read. If several of these sound familiar, a primary care doctor is a good, judgment-free place to start.

**Can a supplement like DHM let me drink more safely?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM or any other supplement makes heavy drinking safe or lowers the long-term risks of alcohol, such as cancer or liver disease. DHM has interesting research on alcohol metabolism and hangovers, mostly in animals with limited human data. Some people use it on nights they've already decided to drink moderately, but the limits in this guide apply no matter what you take.
